items.title: Mao Zedong and China's Cultural Revolution (3/3) | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>From peasants' son to revolutionary leader — Mao Zedong laid the foundation for modern China. This three-part documentary offers an in-depth look at one of the most influential figures of the 20th century.

The legacy of the "founding father" of the People's Republic of China remains deeply controversial. Revered in Europe as a revolutionary icon in the late 1960s, Mao led China to the brink of disaster and ultimately clung to power with a regime of terror. Yet today's leaders in Beijing continue to draw on the cult of Mao. China is now a global power, a transformation that would be difficult to imagine without Mao Zedong.

When Mao Zedong was born in 1893, nothing hinted at his meteoric rise to power. The son of a farming family, he grew up during a period of political instability and profound social upheaval. The 1911 Revolution, which marked the beginning of the end of imperial rule, awakened his mind to politics. At first, Mao had no clear political program. But the Russian Revolution of 1917 introduced him to Marxist ideas, and he soon became a co-founder of the Communist Party of China.

Mao rose steadily through the party ranks as conflict with the nationalist Kuomintang party intensified into a bloody civil war. The devastating retreat that became known as the "Long March" went down in history to become the foundation of the cult of Mao. After World War II, the struggle for power in China continued until Mao and his forces finally reached Beijing.

This three-part series traces Mao Zedong's journey from peasants' son to revolutionary and architect of modern China — from his rural childhood to the founding of the People's Republic to the devastating impact of the Cultural Revolution in the 1960s, which claimed millions of lives.

Archival footage, as well as interviews with historians and eyewitnesses, tell the story of the man who changed China forever.

Today Henri Matisse’s the red studio is considered one of the landmarks of modern art, seen by thousands of visitors at the Museum of Modern art in New York. 
But before arriving there in 1948 it spent more than a decade hanging in a London nightclub.

When Matisse painted the red studio in 1911 it was one of the strangest pictures anyone had ever seen - a room almost completely consumed by red – furniture reduced to outlines, paintings hanging on walls that barely seem to exist, and a grandfather clock with 12 numbers but no hands. Even Matisse wasn't entirely sure what he had created and nobody wanted to buy it.

So how did a painting that even its creator struggle to understand, go from rejection and obscurity to becoming a masterpiece of modern art and what was it doing in a London nightclub in the first place?

items.title: The housing crisis in Los Angeles - Between homelessness and luxury real estate | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Los Angeles' housing crisis is escalating dramatically. Those who can't find a place to live have to get creative — otherwise, survival becomes a daily struggle.

Even before the devastating fires of January 2025, affordable housing was in short supply in Los Angeles. Even people earning an average full-time salary are at risk of ending up on the streets. In 2024, the number of homeless people in Los Angeles County was well over 75,000. The chronic housing shortage is driving residents to get creative, while also giving rise to new business ideas: Gregory sells camper vans to working people who can't afford to rent an apartment. He came up with the idea after he himself had to live in a camper van for a while. Car mechanic Roy also lives in a mobile home. The 64-year-old has to supplement his modest pension by working at an auto repair shop.

Since 2012, Elvina, who immigrated to the US, has been renting out beds in large communal dorms for 55 dollars a night. items.author: Quanta Magazine
items.content:
<article>We know all about how things exist in the three dimensions of length, width, and height. Physicists often talk about time as a fourth dimension, but what if there were a fourth spatial dimension — another direction entirely? How on earth would we picture that? Mathematician Maggie Miller explains why our intuition about three dimensions breaks down in four, and how she visualizes 4D spaces as a reel of three-dimensional snapshots.'

Watch the companion video "How to 'See' the 4th Dimension with Topology"  to learn more: https://youtu.be/MURzTFRRuJQ

“The Joy of Why” is a Quanta Magazine podcast about curiosity and the pursuit of knowledge. The mathematician and author Steven Strogatz and the cosmologist and author Janna Levin take turns interviewing leading researchers about the great scientific and mathematical questions of our time.  For more episodes visit Quanta Magazine: https://www.quantamagazine.org/tag/the-joy-of-why/

---------

Mathematicians use topology to visualize abstract spaces in higher dimensions. Maggie Miller at the University of Texas at Austin explores what happens when knots encounter an extra dimension. Familiar tangled loops behave in unexpectedly complex and counterintuitive ways in 4D: Knots can always come undone, while ordinary surfaces like spheres can — surprisingly — become knotted in ways that can’t be undone.

In this episode, Miller explains to co-host Janna Levin why 4D is the lowest dimension that mathematicians still don’t fully understand, how she and her collaborators resolved a question about knotted surfaces first posed by mathematician Charles Livingston in 1982, and how her interest in art has helped her develop the visual techniques she uses to picture 4D spaces.

items.title: The Global North taken to court - Who pays for the climate catastrophe? | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>From their lecture halls to the International Court of Justice. Law students from the South Pacific have joined island nations to demand greater climate accountability from industrialized countries.

The case before the world's highest court was initiated by 27 law students at the University of the South Pacific, all from islands that could become uninhabitable as sea levels rise and storms grow more frequent.

As might be expected, the Global North has pushed back against their demands for greater responsibility for the consequences of climate change. The United States and Germany argue that international climate law doesn't clearly make countries responsible for past emissions. The young law students are going up against opponents who know the international stage inside and out. What gives them the courage and determination to keep going?

In 2023 they achieved an early victory: their campaign for climate justice won the support of the U.N. General Assembly. That lead to a resolution calling for the international community to take action on climate change.

We follow Vishal from Fiji and Jule from Germany. Both are fighting for justice and compensation for climate-related damage in developing countries. Their journey takes them into the world of international diplomacy, where they confront powerful opponents — among them industrialized nations and oil companies who don't want to have to pay out billions in reparations. All the while, lobbyists and diplomats from major nations try to sway the voices of small island states.

The film captures the optimism of these young people who, full of determination and hope, demand accountability on behalf of the generations to come. Exclusive interviews with judges and historical footage highlight the importance of the case. In July 2025, it all culminates in an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice.
